name: Wonders
lines: The Hall of Wonders
the Wonders of the World
Who built it, when and why
The engineering and the work
The place on the map, then and now
What survives, and how the rest was lost
The evidence: old writers and archaeology

The Great Pyramid was built for a king of Egypt called Khufu, about 4,500 years ago. It was his tomb: a giant stone house for his body and his spirit after he died. It is the oldest of the Seven Wonders, and the only one still standing.

It is made of about 2.3 million stone blocks. Most weigh as much as two cars. Workers dragged them on wooden sledges, and poured water on the sand in front so the sledge slid more easily. The outside was covered in smooth, shining white limestone.
It stands at Giza, on the edge of the desert, just outside the city of Cairo in Egypt. Two more big pyramids and the Great Sphinx stand beside it. The River Nile is close by.

Long ago the pyramid was white, smooth and pointed. Today you see big steps, because people took away the white outer stones to build houses and mosques in Cairo. It has also lost its top. It is about 8 metres shorter than when it was new.

We know a lot because the pyramid is still here and people can measure it. The Greek writer Herodotus visited Egypt about 2,500 years ago and wrote down what he was told. Archaeologists have found the town where the workers lived, and even a diary of a boatman who carried its stones.

The story says King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon built a garden on tall terraces for his wife, Queen Amytis. She came from green mountains and missed them, so he made her a mountain of trees and flowers in the middle of the flat, hot city.

The writers say the garden was built in steps, like a giant staircase. Each step was strong enough to hold deep soil and big trees. Workers lifted water from the River Euphrates to the top with machines, so it could run down and water every plant.

Babylon was a huge city beside the River Euphrates, in the land between two rivers called Mesopotamia. Today its ruins are in Iraq. The land there is flat and hot, so a green mountain-garden would have been a marvel.
Nothing of the gardens has been found for sure. Some people think they were somewhere else, and some think they were only a story. It is the one wonder that might never have been real!

Only writers who lived long after tell us about the gardens. None of them say they saw them with their own eyes. Herodotus, who wrote about Babylon, does not mention them at all. So we must think carefully about what to believe.

The Temple of Artemis was a giant marble house for the goddess Artemis, in the city of Ephesus. It was so beautiful that people came from far away to see it. A man burned it down to make himself famous, and the people built it again even bigger.

It had 127 marble columns, each as tall as a six-storey building. To move such heavy stones, the builder Chersiphron put metal pins in the ends of each column and let oxen roll it along like a giant rolling pin. The temple stood on soft, marshy ground, which helped it survive earthquakes.
Ephesus was a busy port on the coast of what is now Turkey. Today the sea has moved away, and the temple's place is a quiet marshy field near the town of Selçuk.
Today only one column stands, put back together from broken pieces, often with a stork's nest on top. Some of the temple's carved stones are in a museum in London.
Old writers like Pliny measured the temple and wrote it down. Then in 1869 a man named John Wood dug in the mud for years and found the temple's floor and broken columns.

At Olympia, where the first Olympic Games were held, there was a giant statue of Zeus, king of the Greek gods. He sat on a throne, and he was made of gold and ivory. The sculptor was a famous artist called Phidias.

Inside, the statue had a wooden frame. Thin carved ivory made his skin, and sheets of gold made his robe and hair. Workers poured olive oil into a shallow pool in front of the statue to keep the ivory from cracking.
Olympia is in a green valley in Greece, beside two rivers, with hills and trees all around. It was a holy place, full of temples, treasure houses and the stadium where the races were run.

The statue is gone. It was probably taken to the city of Constantinople and burned in a fire long ago. The temple fell down in earthquakes. Its huge columns still lie on the ground where they fell, like stacks of giant coins.

A traveller called Pausanias saw the statue and wrote a long description. Coins from the city show what it looked like. Archaeologists even found Phidias' own cup in his workshop, with his name scratched on the bottom!
Mausolus was a ruler who lived long ago. When he died, his wife Artemisia built him a huge, beautiful tomb. It was so famous that today any grand tomb is called a 'mausoleum' after him.

It had a tall stone base, then a ring of 36 columns, then a roof shaped like a pyramid of 24 steps. On the very top stood a stone chariot pulled by four horses. Four famous sculptors each carved one side.
Halicarnassus was a harbour city on the coast of what is now Turkey. Today the town is called Bodrum, and it is famous for its blue sea and white houses.

Halicarnassus stood on a bay on the Aegean coast of Caria, in south-west Asia Minor; today it is Bodrum, in Muğla Province, Turkey. Herodotus, 'the father of history', was born there about 484 BC. Mausolus laid out the city round its harbour like a theatre, with the tomb on a terrace in the middle of the slope, where everyone in the harbour could see it.
Earthquakes broke the Mausoleum. Later, knights took its stones to build a castle by the harbour, which still stands. Today there is only a big hole with some broken stones where it stood.
The Roman writer Pliny described it. Then an archaeologist called Charles Newton found the spot and dug up pieces of the statues, horses and carvings, which you can still see in a museum.

The people of Rhodes won a war, so they built a giant bronze statue of their sun god, Helios, to say thank you. It was about as tall as a ten-storey building. It only stood for about 54 years before an earthquake knocked it down.

Workers made an iron frame, like a skeleton, and filled parts of it with heavy stones. Then they covered it with plates of bronze. As it got taller, they piled earth around it to make a hill to stand on, and took the hill away at the end.
Rhodes is a sunny island in the Aegean Sea, in Greece. Its city had busy harbours full of ships. The Colossus stood near the harbour, where sailors could see it.

Many pictures show the Colossus standing with one foot on each side of the harbour, with ships sailing between its legs. That is a myth! It would have been impossible to build, and no old writer says it. Nothing of the statue is left today.

Writers like Pliny saw the broken statue lying on the ground and wrote about how huge it was. No picture made while it stood has survived, so artists today must use clues to guess what it looked like.

The Lighthouse of Alexandria was a very tall tower on a small island called Pharos, beside the great city of Alexandria in Egypt. At night a fire burned at the top to guide ships safely into the harbour. It stood for over 1,500 years!

It was built in three parts, one on top of the other: a square bottom, an eight-sided middle, and a round top where the fire burned. Inside was a long sloping ramp, so animals could carry wood all the way up for the fire.
Alexandria is a big city on the Mediterranean Sea in Egypt, where the River Nile meets the sea. The island of Pharos is now joined to the land, and a fort stands where the lighthouse once stood.

Earthquakes slowly broke the lighthouse. About 550 years ago, a sultan built a strong fort in the same spot, using some of its stones. Divers have found huge blocks and statues from it lying under the sea.
The Greek writer Strabo saw it and wrote about it. Later, travellers from the Arab world climbed inside it and described the ramp and rooms. Pictures of it are on old Roman coins from Alexandria.
What are the Seven Wonders?

Long ago, Greek travellers made lists of the most amazing things people had built. The favourite list had seven. Seven was a special number for the Greeks. Only one of the seven, the Great Pyramid, is still standing.
The Great Pyramid is very, very old. It was already about 2,000 years old when the other six were built! The Colossus stood for only 54 years. The Lighthouse stood for more than 1,500.
How historians know
Historians are like detectives. They read what old writers said, look at what archaeologists dig up, and check if the clues agree. When clues are missing, a good historian says, 'We don't know yet.'
